entities.name: Peloponnesian War
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Peloponnesian War (430–404 BCE) was a devastating conflict fought between Athens and Sparta, two of the most powerful city-states in ancient Greece. This war, which lasted for nearly three decades, had far-reaching consequences for the region, including the decline of Athenian power and the rise of Thebes as a major force in Greece.

The war began in 431 BCE, when Athens, seeking to expand its influence, invaded the city of Amphissa in Thessaly. Sparta, responding to this threat, allied itself with the Persians, who were seeking to reclaim their lost territories in Greece. The war saw the rise of new military leaders, such as Alcibiades and Lysander, who would go on to shape the course of Greek history.

One of the most significant consequences of the war was the decline of Athenian power and the rise of Thebes. The war also saw the devastating effects of the plague, which ravaged Athens and led to the deaths of an estimated one-third of the population. The war finally ended in 404 BCE, with the defeat of Athens and the imposition of a peace treaty that would have far-reaching consequences for the region.

The Peloponnesian War is a testament to the complexities and nuances of ancient Greek history, and its legacy can still be felt today. As historian Donald Kagan has noted, the war marked a 'turning point' in Greek history, as it 'marked the end of the golden age of Athens and the beginning of a new era of conflict and instability in the region.'
